title: Bit manipulation: bitwise operators, tricks and bitmasks in Python — cv.cm
description: Bit manipulation explained: AND, OR, XOR, NOT and shifts, common tricks like x & (x - 1), bitmask subsets, Python code with outputs and pitfalls.
h1: Bit manipulation explained: operators, tricks and examples
answer: Bit manipulation means working directly with the binary digits (bits) of integers using bitwise operators: AND (`&`), OR (`|`), XOR (`^`), NOT (`~`) and the shifts `<<` and `>>`. With them you can test, set, clear and toggle individual bits, store a set of small numbers in one integer (a bitmask), and solve problems such as counting set bits or finding the single unpaired number in constant extra space. Each operation is a single fast CPU instruction for fixed-size integers.

body: An integer is a row of bits, and many problems are really about those bits: file permissions such as `rwx`, feature flags, network masks, pixel colors, compact sets of options, checksums and hashes. Bitwise operators let you read and change many bits at once in a single operation, which is compact in memory and very fast.
Interview questions also use bit tricks because they give elegant O(1)-space solutions, for example finding the one number that appears once when every other number appears twice.
Bit positions are counted from 0 at the right (the least significant bit). The mask `1 << i` has only bit i set.

body.note: Operator precedence: in Python, comparisons bind more loosely than `&`, so `x & (x - 1) == 0` works as intended. In C, C++, Java and JavaScript, `==` binds more tightly than `&`, so the same expression means `x & ((x - 1) == 0)`. Always add parentheses: `(x & (x - 1)) == 0`.

body: Brian Kernighan's method clears the lowest set bit until nothing is left, so it loops once per 1-bit, not once per bit position. Trace for x = 44 (binary `101100`):

body.code:
def count_bits(x):
    count = 0
    while x:
        x &= x - 1        # drop the lowest set bit
        count += 1
    return count

print(count_bits(44))     # 3
print((44).bit_count())   # 3
print((44).bit_length())  # 6

body: `int.bit_count()` is available since Python 3.10. `int.bit_length()` returns the number of bits needed to write the number in binary, without the sign.

body.code:
from functools import reduce
from operator import xor

# Every number appears twice except one: pairs cancel out with XOR.
print(reduce(xor, [4, 1, 2, 1, 2]))   # 4

# Swap two integers without a temporary variable (for illustration only).
x, y = 5, 9
x ^= y; y ^= x; x ^= y
print(x, y)                            # 9 5

# Bitmask as a set: enumerate all subsets of 3 items.
items = ["a", "b", "c"]
for mask in range(1 << len(items)):
    print(mask, [items[i] for i in range(len(items)) if mask >> i & 1])
# 0 []
# 1 ['a']
# 2 ['b']
# 3 ['a', 'b']
# 4 ['c']
# 5 ['a', 'c']
# 6 ['b', 'c']
# 7 ['a', 'b', 'c']

body: Mask 0 is the empty set, 5 (binary `101`) is `['a', 'c']`, and 7 is all three items. Bitmask dynamic programming uses the same idea, with a mask as the state, for problems over up to about 20 items, such as the traveling salesman problem on small inputs.
Two more classics: `x & 1` is 1 for odd numbers, and XOR of all numbers from 0 to n with all the values in a list finds the one missing number.

body: A bitmask uses one bit per possible element, so a set of 64 flags fits in a single 64-bit integer, compared with 64 separate boolean variables or list entries.

ul: Negative numbers: Python integers behave as if they had infinitely many sign bits, so `~5` is `-6` and `bin(-5)` is `-0b101`, not a two's complement string. To see 32-bit patterns, mask the value: `-5 & 0xFFFFFFFF`.
Right shift of negative numbers in Python is arithmetic: `-8 >> 1` is `-4`, and `-1 >> 10` stays `-1`.
Overflow in fixed-width languages: in Java or C, `1 << 31` on a 32-bit int becomes negative or undefined; use a 64-bit type and `1L << 40` or `1ULL << 40`.
Confusing logical and bitwise operators: `and` and `or` (`&&`, `||` in C-like languages) return truth values, while `&` and `|` work bit by bit.
Readability: replacing `x * 2` with `x << 1` gives no speed benefit in modern compilers or in Python, and makes code harder to read.
Unix file permissions: `chmod 754` sets three 3-bit groups (rwx = 4 + 2 + 1).
Networking: IPv4 subnet masks, where `ip & mask` gives the network address of a CIDR block.
Flags and options: Python's `re.IGNORECASE | re.MULTILINE` and `enum.Flag` combine options with OR.
Graphics and colors: a 24-bit RGB value packs red, green and blue as `(r << 16) | (g << 8) | b`.
Data structures and algorithms: Bloom filters, bitsets, Fenwick trees (which use `i & -i`), hashing and checksums.
Interview problems: single number, counting bits, power of two, reverse bits, missing number, subsets via bitmask, sum of two integers without `+`.

faq.a: It clears the lowest set bit of x. It is used to count set bits and to test whether a positive x is a power of two, which is true when the result is 0.

faq.q: Why is ~5 equal to -6 in Python?
faq.a: Integers use two's complement, where `~x` equals `-x - 1`. Python applies this to its unlimited-size integers, so flipping every bit of 5 gives -6.

faq.q: How do I count the 1 bits of a number in Python?
faq.a: Use `x.bit_count()` in Python 3.10 or later, or `bin(x).count("1")` in older versions. For negative numbers, `bit_count()` counts the bits of the absolute value.

faq.q: Is bit manipulation faster than arithmetic?
faq.a: For fixed-size integers, bitwise operations are single instructions, but so are addition and multiplication by constants after compiler optimization. The real benefit is compact storage and constant-space algorithms, not replacing ordinary arithmetic.
